utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Lesic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Today we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, Judge Morrison away due to his urgent personal matters. Yes, Ms. West. Please continue. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. May I be heard on one quick housekeeping matter from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You will remember that Mr. Mitchell was discussing with the witness 65 ter 7981. He inadvertently forgot to tender it to the Court. You will remember this was the document regarding Mr. Karadzic's orders regarding the journalists and how they were to travel. I can be -- I can be -- I can speak on its admissibility if there is any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That may be similarly treated as the exhibit at that we admitted as P4407, but can I hear from you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have the same objection that the witness didn't confirm anything about the document, but other than that it's the same issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it for the same reason. That will be admitted as Exhibit P4408.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P4439.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lesic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, yesterday when we had stopped you had mentioned that you travelled to the region between 1992 and 1995 about ten times. Do you remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk a little bit more about that. Now, in general in regard to those trips, how often did you meet with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would presume each time I went there I met with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And how often would you meet with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say half of that time, not every time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at one point in the course of those trips did General Mladic make a request of you regarding a video of General Mladic's daughter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. His daughter passed away, and he asked me could I next time I came back could I provide him a film. He would like to see it. So I said, Yes, I will. So I made a few -- few my trips copies and put all in one film and delivered to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But specifically did he ask for footage of his daughter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, but I give him more than just the footage of his daughter. I give him three or four times that I been there and all those footages.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday you indicated that when you were interviewed in August of 2009, you brought video-tapes with you to the interview. You brought four with you. Do you remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, when you went to that interview in August of 2009, were you shown a video-tape that was not one of the four that you brought with you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was shown, yes. The one that they -- when they raided Mrs. Mladic house they showed me that video that I brought them originally.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So, just to be clear, the video that they showed you that you had not brought, did you recognise that video?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What did you recognise that video to be?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognised my video and I put together, made over, and I give to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So, this was the video you gave to Mladic years ago?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to show you some footage, and this is footage from that video which is a small part of that video. It's 65 ter 45349. This is July 11th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: There's -- Your Honours, there's a transcript in e-court as well. And we're going to show you a short part from minute 26:30 to minute 27:50, and if I can correct myself, 65 ter 45349A.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you see a video in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will see it will come up. It hasn't come up yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, you've seen this video in the last couple days. Do you remember this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting I happened to be there the day before that they came from the Trnovo when they sort of free the Trnovo took over was -- and that was discussion about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And in the screen we see in front of us at 26 minutes 33 seconds, can you identify the people there? The person on the left, who is that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Myself and General Mladic, and I would believe was Koljevic in the back. It's hard to see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Now, this is -- we're going to play it this is video. Is -- was the video camera yours?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And who was operating it at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother-in-law that came with me from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And on the occasions that you used your video camera, when you were actually seen in the photo, was it typical that you gave your camera to someone else to operate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So now we'll play.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the translators could translate this. I know there is a transcript that exists, but it might be easier if they simultaneously translate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The soundtrack is not very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were they given the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: They were. Maybe if we could wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see the -- I'm seeing the transcript in the e-court. Why do you have a redaction there?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, that part's not in this clip. That's the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what we are going to hearing is Mr. Karadzic's words?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: First we're going to hear from Mr. Mladic, then we're going to hear from Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the 65 ter number again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, 65 ter 45349A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in the transcript Mladic's words do not appear.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry for this confusion. The part we'll focus on is Mr. Karadzic's words. Mr. Mladic will speak first and then he will speak. So if I can just play it through Mladic, we don't need an interpretation, and then Mr. Karadzic's speech, if that could be interpreted that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. We are at 26:58, and this is the beginning of Mr. Karadzic's speech. Mr. Lesic, if you can follow along, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Mr. Karadzic: Congratulations to General Mladic and all his commanders, generals, colonels for the success and the speed with which they achieved it. There was a time when we had a very long front line and difficulties with the entire world. That was about Konjevic Polje, Zepa. They thought it was an immense city. It was a village with 3.000 inhabitants. However, they didn't bat an eyelid for Trnovo and there was not a campaign to save Trnovo and to proclaim it a protected area, and that goes to the credit of this army which is as fast as wind. I notice in a Japanese TV series ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to stop right there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Lesic, you heard that speech; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And I know that you've heard it before as well. And Mr. Karadzic's -- can you tell us what event prompted this speech? What was the event this dinner was celebrating?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well job done at Trnovo, and they were so quick and no blinked an eye. That was job well done. President congratulate General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And in particular, Mr. Karadzic is talking about the international community. He says the entire world knew about -- he mentions Konjevic Polje and Zepa, and then he goes on to say, "However, they," the entire world, "didn't bat an eyelid for Trnovo and there was not a campaign to save Trnovo." Mr. Lesic, was the international coverage, the media coverage, of the events in Trnovo less than the others cities that he had mentioned, Konjevic Polje and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely it was. It was said that evening that no one made any comments or anything. Everything went well, was no any obstructions or any discussions that president heard from anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And he goes on to say that there was not a campaign to save Trnovo and proclaim it a protected area. When he says that there wasn't a campaign to save it, who did he believe would support the campaign? Who would have been behind that campaign, from your experience and your presence at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way I understand it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe this is calling for speculation on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you reformulate your question, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, when you first came to the area in December of 1992 and you went to the Assembly session meeting, you specifically gave some money to media and propaganda, and you talked about this yesterday; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so was the issue of international -- the international media coverage of the area one that was of concern to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was concern to all of us. Like media was always against the Serbs and was never in the middle, and that's what we all in Canada or in Serbian Republic believed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And had you had discussions about this concern with the leadership in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I mentioned to them and what can we do about it. We had some media from Israel there, but they need sort of funds to be spended travelling and cars and gas and all that to be right time and right places. So we as a Humanitarian Organisation Republika Srpska from Canada we tried to help as much as we could to sort of change that, but it was not that easy.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And earlier today at page 7, line 9, you said it was said that evening no one made any comments or anything. Everything went well. There was no obstructions or any discussions that the president heard from anyone. When you talk about obstructions or discussions the president heard from anyone, with do you mean by that? Can you tell us a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the UN or Western media didn't make a big outcome that Trnovo was fallen back to Serbian hands. That's what -- what we all felt it, that went nice and easy and quiet.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And from that dinner that evening, did you understand that Mr. Karadzic was pleased about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were all pleased. We were all in that room pleased the way it went. That's how I got that impression. We should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: From your discussions with Mr. Karadzic about this issue of the international media, did you understand whether he placed any blame on the media for interfering with the affairs of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, when I was there visiting and talking to different people like Biljana Plavsic and all of them, we all have some comments about the media position they took, that even though in Canada I recall was long time ago, my boys went to school, 10 and 12 years of age, and the media really played if you're Serb, you sort of -- what the heck you people doing over there, that kind of a thinking was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to turn to 65 ter 32769, and this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Before we leave this video, I notice that in the Prosecution's summary of this witness's testimony and particularly in the 92 ter summary that I'm looking at, they've indicated that was said -- what was spoken about on this particular clip involved Konjevic Polje and Cerska, but we received interpretation of Konjevic Polje and Zepa. So I'm wondering which is correct. What did Dr. Karadzic refer to?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think if we were to look at the transcript we might get an answer to that. I think when we heard the translation perhaps it was a little bit different. I did today hear Konjevic Polje and Zepa. I understand in the transcript itself it says Cerska as well. I think we'll have to go back to the clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we try it now again?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Mr. Karadzic: Congratulations to General Mladic and all his commanders, generals, colonels for the success and the speed with which they achieved it. There was a time when we had a very long front line and difficulties -- the kinds -- the entire world knew about Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and as for Zepa they thought it was an immense city, but it was a village with 3.000 inhabitants. However, they didn't bat an eyelid for Trnovo and there was [sic] a campaign to save Trnovo and proclaim it a protected area, and that goes to the credit of this army which is fast as mind. I noticed in a Japanese ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender that video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4440, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We may have 65 ter 32769.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Lesic, this is an intercept from October 10th, 1994. And your -- you've looked at this before. Is this a conversation you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us who initiated this phone call?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I can see it, I believe I called a few times, many times over there with Ned Krajisnik, and with president of humanitarian organisation, Ranko Rakanovic, and we had discussion with different people like General Mladic and his secretary and -- his intelligence, Petar Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what were the circumstances of the call? Why did you call?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we just want to sort of say hello and see how they doing. All different calls go to different times. I can't say right now which call. Was many calls.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. We're going to focus particularly on page 3 of the English, which is the same as the B/C/S. It's the top of the page. And the L is you, the M is Mladic. I'm going to read this small portion out: "Mr. Lesic: Well, now it is time to take advantage of this situation, Iraqi and this situation. "Mladic: I agree. Is it congested there? "Lesic: It is congested, all right. There's 600.000 soldiers. "Mladic: How much, a million? "Lesic: I said America send an army of half a million. "Mladic: What do they want? They want to conquer the world? "Lesic: Well, it certainly looks that way. They want to be the world's police force and Husein is objecting, but for us, this is turning out good. "Mladic: Yes, this is good -- it is good." Mr. Lesic, you remember this call; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I agree with all this that was said.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So now let's just talk a little bit about. It at the very beginning you said it's time to take advantage of this situation, Iraq and this situation. Please explain what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now, sort of media and all other countries were sort of occupied with Iraq rather than Serbian Republic and former Yugoslavia what's happening there. That was my opinion, and I said that will work in our favour, sort of that they left us alone. Just my opinion and that's how we felt it and that's what I told him over the phone.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And towards the end of the conversation you said it's turning out good and Mladic said yes, it is good. Just tell me, good for whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good -- we've been criticised, like, for example, Gorazde and Zepa, all other little bit -- other little villages that was going on. So we were saying now they maybe left us alone. They won't bug us or media or anything like that. They'll be occupied in Iraq, over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Lesic, we're not going to go through the rest of the conversation, but you looked at this transcript the other day. Is this transcript an accurate representation of the entire conversation at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, would I move to -- I would tender this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: -- intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4441.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I suppose it's MFI as usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not our practice to admit it in full when one of the interlocutors testified as to the content?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I understand, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm now going to show another video. This is 65 ter 40567A. Mr. Lesic, this is one of your videos. It's just a small clip of one of them, and it's from August 1994. And we'll just start playing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We stopped at 40 seconds -- 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Were you in this car at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. And I was moving. I was sort of holding camera.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And who else was in the car?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic and the other soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And what were the circumstances of this ride? Why were you doing this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We just went little bit for ride around Han Pijesak, Crna Rijeka, what they call it, and that's about all. He just want to show us a bit around. There was no reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We'll continue to play it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're at 1:28.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is that Mr. Mladic driving the car?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is driving the car at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We've now stopped at 2:29. And as we saw in the subtitles, it said in the Podrinje, we crash them. And here, if the Americans and the English, the Ukrainians, the Canadians in Srebrenica in the meantime, it's the Dutch would not protect them. There is no sound, but it then follows with they would have disappeared from this area a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, this is August of 1994. By this time how long had you known Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two years, I met him first time 1992 in December, and this was in August 1994, about a year and a half or so, year and eight months, two years, close to two years.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what did you understand Mladic's view to be of the international community's involvement in the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that day when we were driving around, he was showing me around and how we are well equipped with the trees and with the -- that we could open a sawmills and that country is so rich, had a granite to sell to Switzerland and all that, that is Turks were not there hundred years, and now he's hoping they won't be there. That was just conversation in that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right we're going to continue to play for just another 40 seconds, and I hope that there's sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lesic, you remember being on this car ride and having this discussion; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4442, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to show you a little bit more video, and this is your footage, but we're actually going to show it from the Srebrenica trial video. It's on another video that we put together. That's P4201. And this is footage from July 16th, 17th and 18th. But before we start, I just want to ask a couple questions. In July of 1995, did you go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what did you bring with you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were a group of asking from Canada. We brought a scanner tube for the hospital in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. You said scanner tube, was this a machine --

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was sort of medical instruments. I tried to get a permit which could be exempt. It was sort of -- gotta wait eight weeks so we got some -- couple husband and wife and they took there as their luggage and they went to Sofia, and two days later when this all arrived three of us came over and we sort of presented to Belgrade hospital, VMA.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And so the scanner that was brought over it was actually brought over by a colleague of yours; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, friends from Toronto.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And those friends put it in their luggage?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how we travelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Now, on July 16th, you said you went to the hospital. Which hospital was this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade called army hospital VMA. It is famous, the best hospital in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And there did you have discussions and was there a conference with Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Was quite a few of us, and we sort of talked about it, and we were congratulated that instruments arrived and president of Humanitarian Organisation Republika Srpska spoke. He was there as well as Ned Krajisnik and I and Mr. Zaroban and his wife and Ilija Rakanovic was six of us from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you film parts of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I believe I did film quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So we're going to show you part of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: For the record, this is V009016 of the Srebrenica trial video. We start at 48 minutes and 55 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this room?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what was that room?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was sort of reception room where we could have a 10, 20 people discussion around the troubles and --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you have the transcript page in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. In the -- in the book itself it begins at 07047906. 7906 is where we're beginning with Mr. Mladic's words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We stopped at 49 minutes and 41 seconds. This looks to be different, not the meeting any more. What was happening here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladic was sort of went to the phone and arranging a two cars for us to drive following morning to Pale to Han Pijesak, Crna Rijeka for six of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you, in fact, videotaped his conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. Whatever shows here I videotaped, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We stopped at 50 minutes and 6 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And here he says you don't have to accepted a car for me. I'll get there. You should send two cars and have them report tomorrow. They should leave in the morning, not tonight. You just mentioned something about cars. Who are these cars for?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were for us, for six Canadians that we arrived with scanner tube from Sofia.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And where were you going the following day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are going on Pale and we are going to Mladic headquarters and Crna Rijeka there just sort of give him some morale and see them all and that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do you know how Mr. Mladic was travelling?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're at 50 minutes and 50 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Lesic, do you know who Vinko is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I just hear the name. He was some kind of a commander somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to stop there, an we're at 51 minute and 22 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, the following day, did you leave Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we left Belgrade. We went to Intercontinental. Met over there intelligence Petar Salapura and another driver from army -- jeep. And six of us left with two cars and a jeep.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. You just mentioned the Intercontinental. That the hotel where you stayed that night?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the hotel we usually stay when we go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When you left the next day you mention the Petar Salapura and another driver from the army. Is this the person who accompanied you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every time we would come, Mr. Krajisnik and myself or anybody else, they give us a sort of a security guard to take us around because we are bringing humanitarian aid so that we know where to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. On the 17th, did you also take footage?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So we're going to continue and we're just going to finish out this footage because I think that will be quicker, and we'll continue on to the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're at 52 minutes and 45 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you recognise this room?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a room where General Mladic in Crna Rijeka was staying, as far as I know, and we were in that room, always invited having a coffee, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the person we see on the screen right now, who is that, the one who is speaking?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is Ranko Rakanovic, president of Humanitarian Organisation Republika Srpska that we have started organised and registered in 1992 and we got our registration 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So he was one of your colleagues; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the person to his right who is in the middle of the screen, who is that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's his brother, Ilija Rakanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the person to Ilija's right on left-hand side of the screen, who is that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's moved away from my screen. I can't recognise.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask you when we see it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now we're at 52 minutes and 52 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Who are these two gentlemen on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic and General Milan Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We stopped at 54 minutes and 5 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And here General Mladic said he hopes the area of Zepa will be taken care of in the same way as the area of Srebrenica. At this time, at this moment, what did you understand had happened in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this speech, I presumed that Srebrenica was sort of conquered, take over, two or three days before our arrival.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And prior to the speech, had you heard anything else about Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just on travelling from Belgrade to Han Pijesak, Crna Rijeka. We had to turn to Bratunac, go little bit around half an hour away, rough road was, so that we avoid our intelligence. Petar Salapura was driving with us says we better go the other route. Someone could come out from the forest. It's safer for us to go back around by the Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what was the normal route that you typically took from Belgrade to Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normal route was that sort of you could go the better road and much straighter, much quicker, but then that incident we took a bit a round route to be safer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, if you remember, you said you can go the better road much straighter, much quicker. Do you know where that went?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not exactly. I wasn't driving, but we went to the sort of -- not to Bratunac but to the -- to the farther straighter. I can't recall the --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- cities.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. We'll continue playing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're at 55 minutes and 42 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And General Mladic is saying thank you for helping us solve our problems regarding Srebrenica and congratulate you, both you and us, on the occasion of the liberation of the Serb Srebrenica. At that meeting what problems did you understand they had in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't understand any of the Srebrenica. He was here more saying that he thank us for bringing that scanner tube when he approached me. I didn't understand anything about Srebrenica here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lesic, yesterday you spoke about the type of media you watched when you were in Canada. In the days leading up to this trip in July 1995, were you watching Serbian television from the region for your news?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was watching on a satellite dish that was showing from Belgrade or Bijeljina or from somewhere what was going on over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're at 57 minutes and 10 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And here General Mladic says half the world attacked us through the Croats and the Muslims because almost half of the world has been helping them. What did you understand half the world to indicate? What did you mean that half the world was helping them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he was saying he was sort of happy that we were together and we brought humanitarian help. We are concerned what's happening in those area, and six of us arrived. He was saying half of world, half of world, in other words -- well, rest of the Western world was against them. That's what they felt at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And we're not going to continue to play this video, but it goes on for a bit, and this is on the 17th. On the night of the 17th, where did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say I -- as I can remember, I slept there at the Crna Rijeka in a bunker as usual when I don't travel same day back to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So at Crna Rijeka they had at least a facility where guests could sleep, where you could sleep?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They had quite a few beds and underground there. It was quite nice apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And the following morning on the 18th, did you have breakfast at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had something, coffee or something. I don't recall. It was long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went farther. As far as I know today, we went to see President Karadzic and his -- and his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And was that in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. That was only short 15, 20 minutes' drive.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to show you some photos, Mr. Lesic. And when you gave the interview in August of 2009 to the OTP, you brought not only videos with you but photos; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you brought many. I think you brought over 30 photos with you, and I'm just going to show you some to at least get a sense of how many trips you took. So we're only going to look at some of them.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 21939A. And the first photo we're going to look at ends in the numbers 7196.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this photo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Was this your first trip?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one, yes. It was my first trip where we are five of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. If you can go from left to right, tell us who these people are?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic, President Karadzic, myself, and General Milan Gvero, and Ned Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I tender this photo, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4443, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We can go same 65 ter number photo ending in 7204.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you remember where this photo was taken?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At President Karadzic's reception or his office or somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: In early 1993, did you have an occasion to meet Mr. Karadzic in New York?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did meet him twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we came from Canada, four of us, to give him support. They had a hell of a time with UN negotiations and all that. They were there two or three days, and we went there to spend with them two days or so. We drove over, four of us, sort of talk to them, help them. We felt -- I was self-employed and we felt we had enough time, Ned Krajisnik and myself and others, to go there and give them support.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you identify the people in this photo, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ned Krajisnik, Dr. Karadzic, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'll tender this one, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is a part of a compilation of nine photos. Are you tendering each photo separately?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If it's easier, they can be all one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If there's no objection, we'll admit it in one. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, in principle, we would prefer that only the photos that are discussed with the witness be admitted. So if she intends on going through each one of them, then you can admit them all as one, but if you are going to select just a few, we would ask that those be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Show us the photos you want to tender and then we will admit them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Then we'll now go to 7212.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is dated October of 1993. Do you recognise this place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Where is this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is at Crna Rijeka, Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And if we can start from the left-hand side and go down the table, can you tell us who's there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Myself, Milan Gvero, Ned Krajisnik, General Milosevic, Marko Sandal from Canada, General Mladic, and Mrs. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to 7216. This is in 1994. What room is this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in Pale at -- either at Momcilo Krajisnik office or President Karadzic office. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But the map on the wall --

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Map on the wall is President Karadzic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Office.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And on other occasions that you were in that office, had you seen that map before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. If we can go around the table and tell us who's there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mile Jelicic, he came from Belgrade with me, my brother-in-law, and that was a lady - I don't know her name - she's some kind of a worker there, secretary of Mr. Karadzic, myself, Momcilo Krajisnik, and President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we could have 7220, please. This is December 1994. Do you recognise this room?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What room is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is at Pale as well, at the President Karadzic headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you start from the left and go around the room and give us the IDs.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deyan Zaroban from Canada, Toronto, Momcilo Krajisnik, President Karadzic, myself, and soldier down there I don't remember his name --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or the two people turned back to me I don't remember them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, fair enough. If we can go to 7238, please. And this is 18 July 1995. Where was this taken?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was taken in Crna Rijeka outside at the picnic table.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And go from the left to right. Can you give us the identifications?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Zaroban from Canada, Toronto, General Mladic and General Momcilo Perisic and Ned Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 7242. This is also July 18th, 1995. Where was this taken?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was taken same place, Crna Rijeka, Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And go from left to right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milan Gvero, Ilija Rakanovic from Canada, Ned Krajisnik from Canada, and Ksenija Zaroban.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that house is in the background. What is that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the back of the -- their back -- Ned Krajisnik back this is entrance going upstairs to the office and reception.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 7250, please. This is from January 1996. Do you recognise this room?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- yes. This is in Crna Rijeka, Han Pijesak, up on the first floor up going to steps, myself, General Mladic, Petar Salapura intelligence, and Ned Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right a number of times you have seen Han Pijesak and Crna Rijeka together. Can you tell us what the difference is between the two places?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Han Pijesak is called all region. There is a region, Han Pijesak, and Crna Rijeka is a little bit farther that is in the mountains under the mountain build.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So when we saw photos where there are woods, is that Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is that the place where you stayed overnight?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the building we saw in the background is that the place where General Mladic would stay overnight?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, while I was there, he did, yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move to -- I would tender these photos as one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be all included in Exhibit P4443. Added to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So only those photos shown will be admitted, added to the exhibit. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Your Honour, at this point I'd like to move to an area upon -- I would like the witness to speak and it's an area that takes place in 2001 and 2009, and I believe the subject matter is relevant to the indictment. I know the Defence is of a contrary position. And I know it may be an issue. I looked at your Ruling yesterday, and you ordered the Prosecution to focus on parts of the evidence were relevant to the indictment. It is my position they are relevant to the indictment, but if I may be heard I'd like to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we would also like to be heard and outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. So, Mr. Lesic, if you could excuse yourself for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In 2001, several years after these events that we've been talking about, the witness met with General Mladic and Mr. Karadzic in Belgrade and in Bosnia. There is a photo reflecting a dinner that the witness had with General Mladic and then the witness would give evidence that following that he went to the area where General Mladic was hiding, and then the following day he went to an area where Mr. Karadzic was hiding. As you recall this is a period of time where the two -- their whereabouts were unknown. I believe that in addition to this, the witness will also tell us about early 2009 when he was home in Canada and he was at a church event and Ned Krajisnik, the person who's colleague involved in this organisation, came to him with Mr. Karadzic's niece, and Mr. Karadzic's niece asked whether Mr. Lesic would organise a fundraising banquet at the church to raise money for Mr. Karadzic. I believe that these events in 2001 and 2009 are relevant to the indictment because they go to the nature of the relationship between Mr. Lesic and the leadership of the Republika Srpska and that's important because if we were -- if we understand that in 2001 and 2009 General Mladic and Karadzic reach out to this witness at a very risky time, that they reach out to this witness, it shows the strength of their relationship thereby giving weight to the impressions and observations that this witness has testified about that he made in 1992 and 1995. And my argument is that if Mr. -- had Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mladic not reached out to Mr. Lesic in those following years, you might be left with some notion that the relationship they had during 1992, 1995, was not so substantial, but because they reached out at a time that was very risky for them, I would suggest that it's relevant to show you that the relationship they had was a very strong one, and that's why I think that these events are important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, could you give me the examples of impressions and observations that Mr. Lesic has testified about --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- what he made in 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: For example, we spoke -- much of the time we have been speaking about the international community and the media and the propaganda that was going on. And Mr. Lesic testified that in June of 1993 at this Trnovo dinner there was this speech from Mr. Karadzic. Several times Mr. Lesic has talked about what Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic's view was of the international community getting involved with their war and what their impressions were about the media and the propaganda and the bias that they believed was going on in international media. Now, this was an opinion that was shared by this witness as well, but several times he has indicated to you that they also had this impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's just something I'd like to say and then I'll hand over to Mr. Robinson. Money wasn't requested for Radovan Karadzic but for the services that isn't being paid for by the court, various services in Belgrade. It wasn't for Karadzic and that is not what the witness said. Mr. Robinson could now take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This is a very thin reed upon which the Prosecution wants to bring in inadmissible evidence. The relationship between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Lesic is absolutely irrelevant to anything that he's testified about. We're still wondering really why he's here at Dr. Karadzic's trial. I can see why he would maybe want to come for -- or wanted -- be wanted for General Mladic's trial but he hasn't offered any evidence about Dr. Karadzic other than what was shown on the video-tape, and we can all see what Dr. Karadzic said. So any relationship that Mr. Lesic had with Dr. Karadzic is completely irrelevant. And we're not contending that he's untruthful in bringing his video-tapes and showing us what was said at the time. So I don't think that you can bootstrap otherwise inadmissible evidence by trying to establish a relationship that is of no moment to the witness's evidence or to the Trial Chamber's deliberations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to reply, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the time, the Chamber will take a break now for half an hour. We'll rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, the Chamber is not satisfied that the portions you referred to are relevant. The objection is sustained. Shall we bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to commend Ms. West for the way that she brought that issue up in advance to the Chamber so that we could deal with it before -- outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber appreciates it as well as. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're waiting, yesterday the Prosecution filed a motion concerning our access to materials in a completed case involving Vasiljevic, and I wanted to let you know that we won't be responding to that motion and we don't oppose the relief that they seek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies for your inconvenience, Mr. Lesic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, could you repeat your last words.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Lesic, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Lesic. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. I'd like to thank you for meeting with us, for meeting with me and the Defence. I hope this will be of assistance to us. I hope it will assist me to put brief questions to you and receive brief answers so that we can finish within the time allocated. Thank you again. Mr. Lesic, you left Yugoslavia because you objected to the previous regime that imposed restrictions on you in economical and political terms. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that was the case. Economical, better life somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that you operate as a Serbian diaspora society in Canada, is it true that in a democratic Serbia you recognised us in 1995 as being a new democratic force that would be fighting on behalf of democracy and that would be fighting against a one-party system. Was that your understanding of the situation, and did you support the political efforts we were making?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic. We supported. As I recall, we give you and Mr. Krajisnik and Biljana Plavsic membership as well from our Humanitarian Organisation Republika Srpska, and at that time in Pale I said, well, it is a good news. We have charted that Canada recognise Serbian Republic after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to dwell on the previous war period. We had the support of the diaspora from the democratic world. Do you remember that at that time we strove to preserve Yugoslavia -- or, rather, we strove to have Bosnia remain within Yugoslavia, whatever the extent of that state?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In diaspora Serbian community in Toronto, Canada, all different cities, we supported all your work and Serbian Republic and to stay in Republika Srpska. We supported the effort at that time what was happening, what was going on. We were all enthusiastic and with you that's how we put ourselves. We had 420 members Humanitarian Organisation Republika Srpska to help your cause and to bring humanitarian help because we supported you at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would still like to deal with the pre-war period. Prior to the war breaking out, did you notice that we were in tolerant in relation to the Muslims, or would you agree that we wanted the Muslims to remain together with us within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with you, sir, that we want to go together with Muslims and with Yugoslavia. We did not want a war with them. That was discussion, and that was our opinion as well before the war breakdown, but political field didn't let us do that direct -- that way. We were all aware that was an ideal thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Among the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs, did you notice anyone having shown their tendencies of any kind in relation to the Muslims or the Croats, or would you agree that we were an openly democratic community?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. During my visit over there and discussing with intelligence Petar Salapura, he was telling me during a car ride from Belgrade to Pale that we had some Croats and Muslim forces, individuals, going on our side and being with us during that time. I was surprised, but that's what they tell me, that we want -- that that's what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 10, a question was put about Trnovo today, and something with relation in relation to Trnovo was shown. I praised the army for having acted expeditiously. Do you remember something in relation to the declaration of the protected zones of Zepa and Srebrenica? Prior to that declaration there was a large-scale Muslim offensive that was launched against our territory, and at the time no one criticised them for doing this, and what I have in mind above all is the media that you could follow in Canada.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that very well, that Trnovo was quite difficult, that the Muslims was Muslim area one time, and another time they did kick Serbs out that I recall, and I was talking to some people in the media as well, and then as you were praising General Mladic how well job was done, quick and with no any consideration from the West, nobody blinked an eye, and so on. That was not -- that was my understanding at that time, but I was occupied. I was new there. I really didn't know half of it, what was going on. I stay here a night, a day here, a day there. I wasn't very much involved in all that discussion, just what I know, that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and so on and so forth, do you remember that before our counter-offensive, there was a Muslim offensive from Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica? And do you agree that the international media didn't attack them for having launched that offensive. You could hear about that only from our own local media, not from the international media?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic, I would agree with you. That's what I hear from it that no one criticising when they were attacking and when they were sort of on the battle-field against the Serbs. I've been watching that Serbian media and listening to that. I would agree with you all the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that the international media spread propaganda according to which a terrible crime had been committed in Cerska and this continued until General Morillon entered Cerska and showed that this was not the case, denied that that had happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that as well through discussion with the army intelligence that that happened the way you said, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today we had a look at a video excerpt. The date was the 16th, and it was at the VMA in Belgrade. Do you remember what time it was when you went to visit Mladic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time, sir, I'm not aware of the time. I remember that we came from Sofia first day in VMA, and I don't recall the time unless video or picture shows otherwise, and from the Belgrade when we -- the scanner arrived, scanner too, following morning we went to Pale. As well, I don't remember exact time. Was in afternoon, as I believe, that we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether one day before the 16th you spoke to General Mladic? Did you speak to him a day earlier, on the phone perhaps? Can you confirm, in fact, where General Mladic was one day earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember where General Mladic was one day earlier. I remember seeing him as -- in Belgrade in hospital, and following day I saw him on Han Pijesak, Crna Rijeka. That's all I remember where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether on the 16th or the 17th there was a conversation of any kind with General Mladic and his entourage, a conversation that concerned people who may have been killed? And when I mention these people who may have been killed, it's in relation to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any discussion over the people being sort of killed or anything like that. No one would tell us anything what was this. I just know that Srebrenica was sort of taken over two or three days prior my arrival there, that's all. They did not discuss with us about those things, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice that they were making some kind of allusions when they talked amongst themselves? Was there anything in the air, if you will, regarding any kind of unlawful killing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I -- as I was talking to the group of people and all that and they were -- everybody had their own discussion, no one told me about any group of killing or separate killing, nothing that I was aware of. I recall seeing many, many buses going and people -- children and women having put on the buses and drove away by seeing from international media, but I don't remember any other discussion that people was telling me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you now whether you followed in the media what had been happening before that. For example, did you hear of the slaughter in Dobrovoljacka Street on the 3rd of May, 1992? Did you hear about that through our media or international media?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That meaning in market square in Sarajevo? Was that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That could be the question too. In 1994, in February, there was Markale I, the first Markale case. What did you learn about that, and what was your understanding of it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was awful thing to learn that this took place, but then later on I hear from Canadian or Western media, French, I would say, Mr. MacKenzie, General MacKenzie was sort of saying that did not happen as they claimed it happened, so General MacKenzie sort of was always down the street and talking the way things went, and he got replaced as a general, and then General Morillon later on took his position, and also he was sort of fair general. He was co-operating with General Mladic, what I was told, and he was also replaced later on. I don't believe that Serbs did that market square in Sarajevo. Maybe I'm wrong, but I don't believe they did through my discussion and through the after founding, that they done that to themselves so that they have a Western media much more against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So even in the Western media was this idea being bandied about, namely that this crime had been staged, rigged, in order to accused the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That was possible to be rigged because Serbia had no media on their side. Was everything going against them at that time. And I recall going up and about the Sarajevo meeting general in charge that they were sort of shooting in the Sarajevo, and I was asking them, Is that true what's happening? No, no, no. It is not true. It is just the media. I don't know any more than what I was told over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards aid, you were indeed very helpful, you and all Canadian Serbs. Do you agree that the aid that you brought, the monetary part of that aid, was always handed over to officials in the presence of several individuals and that certificates were issued to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were organised. We had, as I said earlier, so many members in Humanitarian Organisation Republika Srpska, and we carried a letter from committee how to disburse the funds and who to help, and then we had our discretion over there asking Biljana Plavsic and asking other officials where it's most needed, and we try to give to the places that's most needed at their suggestion. We were strangers. We were out there. We didn't know where what. We went to hospitals. We went here and there. We always got a receipt. We always got sort of kind of a gramata [phoen] certificate that we have. Yes, we have give funds where we supposed to and that was always spended or used properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you gave it to the final beneficiaries, the end beneficiaries; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We give to the Red Cross in one case. In other cases, we give to the parliament. In other cases, we give to the treasurer of army for soldiers to have their meals or whatever, and one time we have given cigarettes. That what they most needed. And Biljana Plavsic suggested to me they should get some cigarettes, and we brought -- we found it somewhere, and we give them what we could. And we really put ourselves in -- some kind of a tiring spot and flying with helicopter but just to help needy. That was our decision to do, and that's what we did at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you did not give any kind of financial aid to individuals from the leadership, the civilian leadership, or the military leadership, that would be used for their own purposes? Rather, you gave this aid to people who needed it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What we did we give first time in 1992 in parliament session. My video camera taped it so I could show back home in Canada how did we give the help and how did we disburse the funds. Other times we give for the media 15.000, I give, and we sort of -- we give -- people were waiting in a bake shop. I wish that what that footage would show where there was people waiting for bread, and we were -- I was giving them 10 and 20 Deutschmarks at that time, and I almost was run over, but that was our goal, and that was our aim, to give where it was possible, even give people on the street they are needy, like that incidents in the bakery. Other time, we always give in to -- we delivered a hundred tonne of floor, and 20 tonnes we give to different cities, Banja Luka, Doboj, Prijedor, and so on, as the footage will show wherever there is the movies for those things as well. And we were quite happy when I arrived back to Canada that we did well job done and -- at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you saw how the soldiers were living and how they were receiving food and how people in Republika Srpska lived, do you agree that this was grave poverty, also that the people in the army were barely surviving with a maximum of one or two meals per day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall General Mladic would take me, I would say, hundred or 200 metres away from Crna Rijeka, showing me a farm and some little farmhouses where they had the pigs and chickens and growing and being self-sufficient, and sort of telling me how they are doing themselves to create food and to be not waiting till comes from outside or from anywhere else. When I saw all that, every time we arrived from Belgrade we brought some in the cars as much as we could, sort of bringing some kind of food, smoked meat and all other things just to help everybody in the needs as much as we could. I recall one time I ask -- I saw about 20 or 30 soldier around there watching soccer, and I ask General Mladic could I give them a couple of bucks. He says, No. I would not advise you to do that. I said, Why? He says, Well, I don't want just my army receive some kind of a gift and other doesn't. I replied to General Mladic. I said, Who is close to the fire, he gets a heat. I can't -- after all, you're not boss of my money. I brought it here and I will disturb [sic] as I see fit and I give them a 10 or 20 marks to 20 of them. I felt good about it. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're not talking about the Main Staff now. Now we're talking about other places in the field, the Krajina, for instance, various towns. Did you see what kind of life our people had there and how impoverished they were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw terrible things towards my area. Personally I am from the Krajina and Bihac over there, and that was sort of end of the line, and from Banja Luka they didn't get much help over there, so as I was -- always when I had a chance to go close to Bihac, we delivered some help to them as well. It was from my village few, five or six. They were there, and I saw that they were not -- they were pretty poorly living, soldiers and all that. They had no right uniform on them. They were cold and all that. I made a call to General Mladic, and I said, Look, call Banja Luka and send 20 uniforms over here. These people are completely -- they're cold. They don't have much to wear or anything. So he says, What size? I said, Give me the guy. So I told him size so-and-so and all different sizes. And it was a tough for them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that in such conditions it was also rather difficult to feed large numbers of prisoners of war properly? We could feed them only the way we fed our own army.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I never saw any prisoners, but I was told and I would presume, yes, if you don't have food enough for yourself, you cannot give it away as much either. So it's just going from day to day for survival. I am aware of all that. I recall when I was in Austria 1958, young kid, and we didn't have a good time either waiting to escape to -- waiting to be emigrated to different countries, and that's what I put myself in a position this time. I wasn't in army, so I said now I have a couple of dollars in the pocket, and it's [indiscernible], and I want to help my people as much as I can. Thank you God Canada did well for me and I did well for Canada. So I was in a position with a group of others to give that kind of donation and that kind of humanitarian work. Just to explain, wasn't easy to register humanitarian organisation. At that time we were turned down first time to change our name, and I was persist. I says, No. I would like to be Humanitarian Organisation Republika Srpska, and waited another three to six weeks. We got approval from the Canadian government to receive the charter, and when someone gives like a $10.000 donation, they paying high taxes, so they can claim it, 30 or 40 per cent, depends on each individual's salaries. So when I got visited by Canadian intelligence every time I come back, they say, Well, you took money over there. You did this. You did that. I said, Yes, I did. My taxes are paid, and I spended the money, was clear money, the way I saw fit, and we collected so-and-so on. Wasn't any issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the period you, yourself, spend as a refugee. Did you see for yourself that in Republika Srpska, everywhere, the Krajina included, at the time there were a large number of Serbs who had fled not only from Croatia but also from Central Bosnia? Did you come across them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Canada, yes, I came across with lots of immigrants, being 52 years in Canada, 1992, 1994, up to 2009. I personally employed 7.500 people to work in an auto motor industry parts for the cars, to help them out to get settled. I employ -- I got them the jobs there, and they're still working. Up to now is 8.500 people working in different companies. They all settled. They all good tradesmen and machinists and all that. The owner of the company is pretty happy with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you about when you travelled through Republika Srpska. Did you come across refugees there, people who had fled to Republika Srpska from the Muslim and Croat parts of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I went to visit hospitals and bishop from Chicago, Irinej. They were at Kasindol hospital and there were -- some people fled and I was -- pointed out I wasn't close with them, but they say those people fled and we got to help them and all that, and I've been told yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in the Krajina, Banja Luka, other municipalities, did you notice a considerable number of refugees there? Did you help them as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, they are just outskirts of Banja Luka, Derventa or somewhere, as I recall. We saw quite a bit from Sanski Most and from other there were 80 people in one room, and I saw quite a -- quite a refugees there that they had no place to go. They couldn't go back and all that. It was quite disaster. That's when I -- when we brought them the help. It was quite difficult for them. Yes, I saw all that, and I believe I even took some movies from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that you were quite happy with the distribution of aid that the Canadian Serbs sent through you and that there was no abuse of this aid?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were quite -- quite -- quite agree with you, yes. The aids was never abused. We give to the proper places. We got documentation for it, and I even took the pictures and the movies when we brought the aids to present it back to Canada committee that definitely we give to the right places so -- as well we want to cover ourselves, myself and Ned, that we didn't take to our family or whatever. We give to the place that we supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw a transcript today -- or, rather, an intercept -- or, rather, a video-clip. When General Mladic drove you towards Zepa. This is what I'd like to ask you now: Do you know that on that same road, the Muslim side, although it had been agreed that a convoy should be allowed through, they killed a large number of soldiers on the 4th of June, 1992? Did you hear of that case when we lost these young recruits for no good reason whatsoever? This was an act of deceit altogether.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that General Mladic was telling me as well when one Serbian young guy was put on a stick and burned at that area over there, and when he was showing me Muslim house and another Muslim house and so on, I recall. I was only told what was happening there prior to General Mladic driving me around. Yes, that's correct. All I know what I been told, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you take this seriously, his joke when he said to you that he could give you that forest as a present, or was this sort of playful bragging on his part?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood what he was saying. This was sort of a joke between him and myself. He says, You are well-off in Canada. Come here and you can get all this after the war and all that. And I said, Thank you, sir. No, no, just keep up with work. And that was sort of really just a kidding discussion, was nothing serious about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And also, knowing what had happened in June 1992 with that ambush there, as for what he said to you about the Turks, did you also understand that as a kind of bragging in order to correct the picture a bit with regard to those deaths of ours?
