Quite simply, the atmosphere in the car, was it one that was conducive to bragging, exaggeration, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember my staying over there that was some kind of an ambush from the Muslim side, that they broke the lines, and they came over to the Serbian Republic side where were the lines, and they removed us from one hotel to the other hotel overnight for our safety. It was quite dangerous at that time, so -- I was quite myself in shock, Why did I come here? And I recall that. That's all I know. I wasn't told all other things what was going on, just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the previous years and especially in July 1995, when you came to Republika Srpska, did that involve danger of ambushes, and were measures taken for you to be protected?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every time I came over myself and with Ned Krajisnik or with others we were always given sort of security. We don't know the roads. We don't know the travel. And that was from 2000 -- 1992 to 2000 -- 1995. Was always same sort of security from intelligence, Pete Salapura, but it was much less danger in 1995, as I recall, than 1992 and 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you've mentioned a small road, may I jog your memory? Was it the Zvornik-Crni Vrh-Caparde-Sehovici road and Vlasenica as well? In this way, one would avoid travelling between Srebrenica and Zvornik. Was that that road that you took in order to get to Han Pijesak, although it was a road that was much worse?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, we took farther road from Srebrenica and I ask why I was told we are going to avoid? We didn't go -- we went to the Zvornik or closer, Bratunac, to the Bratunac to avoid danger. That's all I can remember. It's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, you as Serbs from Canada, a country in which there is a culture of democracy, to the best of your knowledge did the Bosnian Serbs do anything for which you would feel ashamed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The media was saying, and from beginning, how Serbs do this, do that, rapes and all other things, killings and everything, and I just couldn't believe it, so I sort of tried to find the true information and truth about it, so I went over ten or some times to see what was going on, and I am satisfied that those things did not happen as they proclaimed, that Serbs were bad as they were painted -- they were painted and accused of. It was difficult those years for everybody, including you, sir, over there with so many meetings and all. I recall, I can't even see you. Out of ten times, I saw you maybe three or five times. You were always somewhere in a meeting or whatever. But that was the job you people had to do, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You confirmed today that you saw me every other time, that is to say you saw me considerably less than General Mladic. Is it correct that you were turned towards the military and helping the military? I'm not saying you personally. I'm speaking of the organisation as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, our organisation, Humanitarian Organisation Republika Srpska, dictate to give the help where it's needed, and as we were going forward and backward and come back with the movies, I saw you, as I will say again, out of ten times maybe four or five times, not all the time, but I saw Krajisnik or others in your headquarters, and mostly every time I saw headquarters of General Mladic, and we give the help -- help and need wherever we could, hospitals and people that they were wounded, and I recall the bishop, we bought some equipment in Kasindol hospital and was a French UNPROFOR there. Actually, they delivered it. We paid it for and they delivered it. Yes, we were sort of trying to do the best we can to spread our help all around wherever is required, but was too difficult and is not enough to go around to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So can we agree that when you were there in July in our area you never heard anything about any killings? When was it the first time that you heard there were killing around Srebrenica? Was that after you returned to Canada, and when was it exactly, and from what media did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was occupied -- my head was occupied and my travelling and business in Canada as well to get the scanner tube over, and after scanner tube arrived two days or something that's when I arrived and I been questioned about the Srebrenica, how come you didn't know, you didn't know. I didn't know. I travelled all night, and I travelled from Sofia to Belgrade. I was exhausted and tired. I didn't heard of any killing or anything until media then carry on and carry on. After few days when I returned to Canada, that was things done in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you first heard reports in the media about this, did that bring to mind all the earlier instances of propaganda in the media you, yourself, could see what it was -- for what it was? So was it the same way of blackening the Serbs, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those things were happening there. Serbs were painted -- painted black even though they weren't guilty. As I recall discussion, if they kill one soldier, they made a big issue out of it, killing 10 or 20, and I question intelligence. What, did it happen? No, that's only a media, Pete Salapura says. Don't believe everything you hear. So it was tough. It was tough for everybody there to know the truth. Somehow we didn't have the finance or anything to have a media, Serbian media or any other media to go there, right, and see what's happening and record it to get some time on CNN or CBC or some other. It's very difficult to get to those stations to tell your side of the story. That's what we went through, and I guess we'll never go through again, I hope we never do again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that there was a general prevailing perception that the Serbs had lost the media war, and was a war also waged in the media that we never actually took part in, and that is probably the reason why we had lost it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the way I understand it, living in a Western country for so many years, media can make you or break you. In Canada, if you run for prime minister or party or president, media is a crucial -- crucial things, and TV and publicity and everything. It was the same in the war. I believe personally that Serbs never had a good media on their side from nowhere at that time. So, yes, I agree we lost the war in the media and could not be any differently. I don't see why, but it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This type of biased reporting, did that provoke in Serbs a bitterness, and did the Serbs in Canada find this difficult to cope with the way that the media portrayed the Serbs and whether you had occasion to see for yourself where all those lies were coming from and what the lies were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lesic, I was advised that you are speaking too close to the microphone. Could you move back just a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. Unexperienced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lesic. Could you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The media in Canada, for a moment I actually believed that first time I went over what was going on. Then went over and I saw for myself, and I even ask and ask over and over, and I was never given that was -- that media was on the right track. We were always, always discriminated. We had no media on our side. Just the way we all felt in Canada was rough for us, as I mentioned earlier, when kids go to school and all that and the war's every hour or every ten minutes on the TV, so people talk about it and that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that how you interpreted the intercept of the conversation between you and General Mladic, that both of you actually hoped that this hunger in the media for sensationalism would be slaked by stories coming from Iraq and that they would sort of leave us aside?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During discussion with General Mladic about that incident, yes. I was really hoping that media would leave us alone because they were occupied with Iraq. Yes. That was my opinion, and I said that to him is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he agreed with you in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He agreed with me. General Mladic agreed with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to ask you the following: Is it possible that regarding this meeting with me in 2001, you were confused and that it would have been a different year? I do understand that it may have been sometime before the year 2000. So is it possible that an error was made in the year?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this serious? Is he opening the door to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I hope not. If you would give me a moment to speak with him about that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I was not aware of the Chamber's decision. May I take advice from Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I wasn't aware of the Ruling and that the extent of things that were excluded was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lesic, I thank you for your evidence, and I hope that you didn't find it too difficult. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Just briefly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You were just asked a short time ago from Mr. Karadzic whether the Bosnian Serbs did anything for which you would feel ashamed. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. When I was in Canada, I couldn't believe that they did anything to be ashamed of, so when I went there and I got different story, so I didn't see anything or found anything that Serbians would be ashamed of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So, Mr. Lesic, do you believe that in 1995 that thousands of Bosnian Muslim men were executed by the Bosnian Serbs in the vicinity of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what media says, but I did not learn from anybody else. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And at page 41 of today's transcript, Mr. Karadzic asked you -- we were talking about feeding a large number of prisoners, and he asked you whether you agreed that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Lesic, you said that's what media said, but I did not learn from anybody else. Did you mean you didn't know at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know. I didn't see anything. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What do you think now, Mr. Lesic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do I think now? Yes, there could be on both sides some of it, but not as much as they proclaimed it to be, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, earlier today you were asked about feeding prisoners of war and specific the question was: "Do you agree that in such conditions it was also rather difficult to feed large numbers of prisoners of war properly? We could feed them only in the way that we fed our own army." And you were answer was: Yes, I never saw any prisoners, but I was told and I would presume, yes, if you don't have food enough for yourself then you can't give away much of it either. Now, earlier today you said that you also gave money to the Red Cross. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we give Red Cross for the medicine to buy from Galenika in Belgrade. In hospitals we give not the big money, $5.000, $6.000 here and there. Was not enough to go around. When we give flour as well later on. We helped as much as we could. But when I said I didn't see prisoners, I didn't see everywhere prisoners, but in one incident when I was with bishop I saw some prisoners there, and when I was giving money, cash money to the people waiting for the bread, I saw there prisoners by the Banja Luka from Sanski Most, from all over. Eighty people or hundred people sleep in one big large room.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One area I didn't see, another area, yes, I did see.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But I want to speak more about the issue of food for prisoners. Are you -- you said you gave money to the Red Cross. You must be familiar with the Red Cross's job of registering prisoners and feeding them and providing for them. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. What -- what we did, we go to the little room and they have their thing even for Montenegro delegate. Six or seven people came from Red Cross from Montenegro to Han Pijesak, and they were Red Cross representative. They brought help. And something like that in Banja Luka or in Prijedor or somewhere Red Cross office. You give them, but we get sort of get the pictures and get the paper certificate, get the receipt for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Lesic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lesic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of this Chamber and the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I ask you, sir, to say couple words in regard of my witness being here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lesic, if you could understand, the Chamber usually does not hear from the witness out of its formality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I want to thank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was very impressed with the witness -- the way witnesses being looked after here and a job well done. They look after these people and witness and all that, asking them how they feel and the hotel and driving back and forth. It is well -- well planned, and I want to thank you all the way I was here treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move to private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are in open session. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm advised that the next witness is not yet in the building and is, in fact, en route. I am trying to obtain as clear and specific information about how much time that will take. I presume it's a matter of minutes, in the order of 15 to 20, but I'd like to get that information as quickly as possible and relay it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the timing, the Chamber is minded to take a two times half an in our break now. So starting from now, and we will have just a bit more than one hour session twice. That may suit the situation. Then we will have a break for half an hour and resume at 20 past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Will you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Obradovic. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. Not a problem at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, would you be able to state your full name for us, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ljubomir Obradovic. I was born on January 30th, 1950, in Visegrad, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General, you've appeared before Judges of this Tribunal before, first as a Defence witness in the trial against General Miletic and others in 2008, and then last year you gave evidence as a Prosecution witness in the Tolimir case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And before coming here to give evidence today, you had a chance to listen to a recording of your testimony in the Tolimir case in your own language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were you satisfied with the accuracy of the recording?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I was to ask you the same questions today that you were asked during your testimony in the Tolimir case, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, pursuant to your order yesterday, we've created a redacted version of General Obradovic's Tolimir transcript, and that's been uploaded as 65 ter 23610. If that could please be a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I commend your promptness very much. Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4444, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And as for promptness, I extend that. That's due in large measure to the support that we work with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, during your testimony in the Tolimir case, you gave some details about your function. You said -- actually, I'll start a different way. General, in your Tolimir testimony, you made to clear that you were transferred to the Main Staff of the Bosnian Serb Army on 1 September 1994. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you described your function at page 11929 of the transcript. You said you followed the operative situation and the situation in the battle-field. You wrote orders, reports, warnings, plans, and followed the operative log-books. Do you remember that as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you just explain to us briefly how you -- how you were able to do that job? What information did you rely on to be able to follow the operative situation, the situation in the battle-field and write orders?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: All of that was done on the basis of regular daily and interim reports that we received from subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And before I move on too quickly, Your Honours, I realise I omitted to read the summary of evidence which I would normally have done before this first question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I will do that now with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I also omitted asking you whether Rule 90(E) is necessary for this witness. It was given at the Tolimir case, so I need your guidance.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed. I think that would be the best way to proceed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, probably you are aware of this already, but I would like to draw your attention to a particular Rule here at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the discretion to oblige you to answer the question, but in such a case the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other another case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I was advised of the same in the Tolimir case by the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And very briefly, the summary of the witness's written evidence as filed is as follows: From September 1994, General Obradovic served as the head of the Operations Department in the administration for operations and training organ of the Main Staff of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation. No interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you hear me when I explained the Rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not getting any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I hope you are now hearing me, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. From September 1994, General Obradovic severed as head of the Operations Department in the administration for operations and training sector of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. His duties included following the operative situation, the situation on the battle-field, and drafting documents which included orders, reports, and plans. General Obradovic explains the command structure of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. He identifies in his written evidence core members of the Main Staff of the Bosnian Serb Army and their various areas of responsibility and competence. He explains the structure of the Main Staff. He sets out the various duties and responsibilities of different organs, including the 67th Communications Regiment, the 10th Sabotage Detachment, the 65th Protection Regiment, and the Department of Civil Affairs. General Obradovic explains the timely and accurate reporting system of the Bosnian Serb Army from the lowest level through the Main Staff up to the president, Dr. Karadzic. He addresses how military directives were prepared with all sectors of the Main Staff taking part in their drafting. General Obradovic will describe the communications methods used by the Army of Republika Srpska. These allowed for immediate contact between military commanders and their subordinates, including forward command posts, located through Bosnian Serb held territory. That's the brief summary, Your Honours. And just your indulgence for a moment to see where I left off.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, General, in relating to the information you relied on to carry out your function. I'd like to ask you for a second about the accommodations of the Main Staff. Can you tell us where the Main Staff of the VRS operated from?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The VRS Main Staff, as the high command, was housed in an area that included an underground facility under the Zep mountain, Crna Rijeka, and the Han Pijesak town.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you be able to describe each of those accommodations in a bit more detail for us in order that the Judges can understand the facilities with a bit more detail, beginning with the last one, Han Pijesak town.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Han Pijesak was the place where two sectors were accommodated, the logistics sector and the organisation, mobilisation, and personnel affairs sector, and for a while the moral guidance, religious, and legal affairs sector was housed there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what kind of facilities were located at Han Pijesak? Can you describe the actual accommodations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part these sectors were housed in a hotel. I can't recall what the name of that hotel was. Some kind of lodge or something like that, but it was a hotel, a catering facility of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now moving on to Crna Rijeka. Could you describe the facilities there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: There were two buildings in Crna Rijeka and subsequently another one. They were built -- they were like cabins, log cabins, and they were there for accommodating the 17th Communications Regiment and also for parts of the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment. The staff sector was housed also in these cabins: The security and intelligence sector, the air force and air defence administration, the planning, development, and finance administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I understood from the interpretation that the buildings the Main Staff was housed in at Crna Rijeka were log cabins. Did you mean to describe wooden structures or something else?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were wooden structures, yes, like huts.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were they prefabricated?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These structures are used for housing personnel. They are prefabricated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I also understood from the interpretation that you also referred to the 67th Communications Regiment -- - pardon me, the 17th Communications Regiment. Did you mean to refer to the 67th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I did say the 67th Communications Regiment, and parts of it were in Han Pijesak, in Crna Rijeka, and also in the underground facility, because its elements were used to provide certain communications assets and types of communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about that underground facility for a moment. First of all, how far from it was your headquarters at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: About 2 to 2.5 kilometres, because the entrance to the facility faced Crna Rijeka. It was on that slope.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And was the underground facility in constant use throughout your time in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: As it was an underground facility, it's not very comfortable. It's not well aired, so it's not a good place to spend time. We would stay there only when threatened with NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The communications facility or a portion of the 67th Communications Regiment was permanently housed there; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How big was the underground facility?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It was divided into blocks. One of the blocks was the technical one, and it had generators for the heating, for ventilation, and for the lighting. There was also a reservoir with drinking water. There was one section or part that was used for the communications regiment, and there was a part used for offices and for accommodation for the number of people involved at that level of command. This facility had been built for the command of the 7th Military District in the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just -- I'd just like to go back to communications for a moment, and I wonder if you can list for us the different means of communication that the Main Staff had available to it throughout your time there.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, communications can be broken down into command communications, co-operation communications, and intelligence communications. You can use radio, the wire, relays. I'm not a communications expert, so I could slip up. As for the equipment, there were automatic telephone exchanges and various types of relay devices. Again, it all depended on whom you had to establish communications with. The communications equipment used depends on the unit that needs to use certain kind of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's just talk about telephone exchanges for a second. How many telephone exchanges did the Main Staff have available to it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did it have a PTT telephone exchange available?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It had an automatic telephone exchange, yes, and there were so-called civil numbers. That's what we called them. That was the case in the corps, and in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did it have a military telephone exchange, military switchboard, available to it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that there were a number of such switchboards. The communications regiment had various types of devices that weren't that large, but as for these fixed exchanges, I think that capacity was far greater, and they had far more extensive series of numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you talked in your Tolimir testimony about extension 155. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was that part of the military -- a military telephone exchange?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'm a bit curious about this three-digit number, actually. This first number, 1, does that -- do people who have an extension with that first number have any specific means of communication available to them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. These are three-figure numbers that each office had or official in a military switchboard, and this had to do with the agreement, the mutual agreement reached between the organs of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You talked about relay devices, different types of relay devices. What did you mean to describe when you referred to them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Radio relays are used by high-level units. We communicate over the phone, but up to a certain relay which then connects to the next relay where the next unit is located, and then the transmission continues towards the phones. These are radio relays, and they can be intercepted. Conversations can be intercepted in spite of the fact that people might be using phone devices, have phones in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you talk about these relays being available to high-level units, from what level are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: From the level of the brigade as a tactical unit and upwards. So the Infantry Brigade, motorised brigades, and other types of brigades that are concerned. The light brigades did not have such equipment as per their establishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony in the Tolimir case, you talked about an encryption device that you referred to as KZU 63. Was that a device that was used to protect the relay communications you've just described?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It could be used to protect radio relays, but it was also used for radio links at a lower level. It would be installed for two participants, for one participant on one device and for the other on the other device. So you compress the information and in a very short period of time the information is forwarded. It is an abbreviation for crypto-protection device 63. The number 63 refers to the model. It is the year in which the device was produced.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was this device part of the normal assets of the corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many such devices the corps had, but they did have such devices.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How would such a device -- or what organ would be responsible for the supply of such a device?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Planning and organising communications in staff sector is done by the communications organ. The implementing communications and having equipment, well, it's the 67th Communications Regiment that should have such equipment at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just by way of an example, in the event of an operation that required the establishment of a forward command post, what would the procurement process be for forward command post to secure one of those devices?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: If we're dealing with the corps forward command post, then when planning an operation, in addition to all the other tasks that concerned assessing enemy strength, engaging one's own forces and equipment and so on and so forth, in addition to those tasks, the communications organ within the corps would plan for certain communications in accordance with the decision of the corps commander. And if it was a plan when establishing the forward command post taken -- or drawn up by the Main Staff, when one functioned within the Main Staff you attempt to get the 67th Communications Regiment, so the communication the organ, to plan for the necessary communications system.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If the forward command post related to an operation that involved one or more corps and was therefore commanded by a member of the Main Staff, what would the procurement process then be? How would they get one of those devices for the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in accordance with the plan for the operation, the last element of an order or a decision that has to do with the commands and communications, and in that part of the order the commander will request the kind of communications that need to be organised, and this will then be the duty for the communications organ from the staff sector. They will have to use the 67th Communications Regiment in order to organise such communications at the forward command post in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. On this subject, actually, I'd like us to look at a document, please, 65 ter 02050, dated 14 July 1995. It's a document bearing the reference number 04-520-56/95 from General Tolimir to -- General Tolimir, who is writing at the time from the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, to General Miletic. And he says: "In order to have a complete review of the Drina Corps command radio network, it's necessary to incorporate the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska in the work plan of the Drina Corps command communication with an RU2/2 radio and a KZU-63 set." Now, relating to what we've been discussing, I have a couple of questions about this document. First of all, can you tell us what an RU2/2 K set is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It's a radio device. 2/2 K, it's a kind of radio device. It's the kind of radio device that we had. A little more modern if compared to a RUP 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say "radio device," do you mean that it's just a radio or do you mean it attaches to and works in conjunction with a radio?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: With your leave, I'll explain the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the heading, you can see that it's the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, and at one of its command posts there is Major-General Zdravko Tolimir. It is obvious that from that location -- it says, "In order to monitor combat activities." That's with it says in the first sentence: "In order to monitor combat activities around Zepa and gain a complete -- gain complete insight into the Drina Corps radio network with brigade commands, it is necessary for the VRS Main Staff to be included in the Drina Corps command work plan for communications, and it should have one radio RU2/2 with encryption, and it says that all brigade commanders have this equipment." So this radio network is protected by these devices. So in order to be able to listen to communications between the Drina Corps and his command brigades, because he was in charge of the operation, he needs such a radio device.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, in your question, transcript page 66, line 14 to 16, I said: "If the forward command post relate to an operation that involved one or more corps and was therefore commanded by a member of the Main Staff." That was your question, and we didn't hear from the witness, and I wonder why don't you put a question to the witness whether the document we are seeing now is related to an operation that involved one or more corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, with respect to the document in front of us which emanates from General Tolimir, do you know, first of all, whether this relates to an operation that involves more than one corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document shows that this operation had to do with the Drina Corps. General Tolimir talks about the operations of the Drina Corps. He talks about this with the brigade commanders. If it concerned two corps or more, if this operation concerned two corps or more, then the Main Staff would have the obligation of leading the operation, and then all these types of communications would have been planned and communication with all the participants would have been made possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, you indicated in your Tolimir testimony that you were on leave from January until the 17th of July, 1995. Now, I wonder after your return to the Main Staff whether you became familiar with the operation that found General Tolimir at the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't become familiar -- well, the date here is the 14th of July. I returned on the 17th of July. I broke my leg on the 27th of January, and I recovered and returned on the 17th of July. But the document shows -- well, I couldn't have even known about this because the Drina Corps planned this operation, and it's the commander who is in charge of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one last question, General: What was General Tolimir doing writing the Main Staff from the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you what he was doing. Obviously he was in a brigade that was subordinated to the Drina Corps. The Drina Corps carrying out the operation. As to whether he received a task from the commander to gain insight into something or not, I don't know. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In what circumstances would one of the assistant commanders normally be deployed to a brigade headquarters as in this situation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In order to supervise certain combat activities, this can also be done in the field. As to why Mr. -- why General Tolimir was there, I don't know. Did he receive an order from the commander or was he simply there and tried to find information and thought that perhaps someone should listen in to the radio network within the Drina Corps in the course of the operation. I don't know what his position was and on the basis of whose order he was down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So one last question before leaving this document. Based on what I just understand you've said, this equipment would enable whoever has it not only to communicate with units of the Drina Corps command but also to monitor those conversations; is that correct? Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If they have or if he has the same encryption device.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have this as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4445, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to go to one further documents and, to change topics, back to the Main Staff and the structures per se, and that's 65 ter number 23594, an organigramme of the Main Staff prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor based on your evidence in the Tolimir case. Now, while we can call this up on the monitors, Your Honours, I think the printing might be kind of small, so we have copies of this in A3 format for Your Honours and for the witness and for the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's very find of you, Ms. Edgerton. I take it there is no objection to the addition of this and other documents to the 65 ter list, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you could just in the fullness of time pass one copy to the witness as well, I'd like to ask him a question about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that he has it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He doesn't have a paper copy, Your Honour, and just so he can see more clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's on its way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, do you remember looking at this organigramme yesterday in preparation for your testimony today, setting out some of the formations and structures of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, at the time, you noted that the organigramme was accurate but for the omission of reference to General Mladic's office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The office, the cabinet, doesn't relate to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where would that fit into this organigramme?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, here to the right. You can see the where the sector for co-operation with foreign military representatives is, so it would be in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who staffed that cabinet, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember, but I do remember Rajko Banduka. He left an impression on me, so I do remember him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember what his job was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was a secretary. I didn't have a secretary, so I don't know anything about the nature of his work.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, having a second look at this document today, did --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. On the whole, he'd make notes, help the commander. He would plan his agenda, receive calls, and so on and so forth. He would sit in the office that was next to the commander's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In the Zep Goljak 1 facility, G1.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one question regarding the commander's office. Did he share that office with anyone?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. That office is at the very entrance into this underground area, as you call it. So this entrance is marked by -- is masked, rather, by this villa, and in this villa there were a few rooms and that's where the commander was and his closer co-workers from the cabinet and from security.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did the commander have an office at each of the three Main Staff facilities you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where was -- where were his offices then? And just to be perfectly clear, when the commander was at the Main Staff, where was that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: He was staying at the entrance at this villa before you enter the underground. When he'd come, he would just go to anybody's office to get some business done, usually at the chief's office or some other close co-worker. Over their barracks, he did not have an office that was particularly his.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've just understood you to say, Over the barracks, he didn't have an office that was particularly his. What do you mean by that? Over what barracks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean there was no office where he would be the only person who would be signature there and nobody else. If you have an office, you are in that office. However, if your boss were to be appointed commander, then he would come to get something done with you, and he'd come to your office to get that done.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've just said there was no office where he would be the only person who'd be sitting there and nobody else, so who did he normally sit with?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, for the most part he was up there, up there, this establishment facility where his room was, his bedroom or the room where he slept and where he worked, and downstairs he'd usually go to see his assistants who were there, or he'd come to that small operations room where we were. I mean, there was not a particular place that had been envisaged for him to be there permanently.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one last question. When you say "he was up there," General, I'm afraid we don't know what place you mean by that. So what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: You insist, or you think that down there where the barracks are in Crna Rijeka, you're insisting on some room that he was staying at all the time. He did not have any such room. When he'd go by car 2.5 kilometres, if he needed to exchange something with someone, then he'd do that with the assistants. If he wanted to visit and check, then he'd see everybody. If he had some business with the intelligence people, then he'd stop by and see them. If he had something to talk to the operations people, us, then he'd stop by our office and see us. So he did not have this particular place where he would come all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to go back to the organigramme, having a second look at this since you last did, the day before yesterday, do you have any information additional that you wish to add to it, anything you feel needs to be filled in to make it accurate?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, nothing. I remembered my testimony in the Tolimir case. The last name of the colonel who headed the communications unit was Gredo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, with that, could we have this as the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4446, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I didn't go through the Tolimir transcript, but I take it he explained the meaning of the dotted line on this organigramme.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He did not, Your Honour, and it's something I'd actually like to come back to in the presentation, which is why I wanted it dealt with up front --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, in your Tolimir testimony you explained the combat reporting system of the Army of Republika Srpska and how it worked from the brigade level right up to the Main Staff. You referred to the Main Staff's reporting obligation to the supreme commander, Dr. Karadzic. You explained how reports were prepared, who prepared them, and how reports from subordinate units were excerpted and incorporated into the Main Staff's report to Dr. Karadzic, and you were shown some examples of this. That's in your Tolimir testimony at pages 11966 to 11982. Do you remember all that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you some additional questions about reporting and then turn to a series of documents. My first question is: Did forward command posts have the same reporting obligation as other VRS units? And I mean forward command posts at all levels.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Forward command posts wrote daily operations reports and combat reports just like all other units for the area for which they had been established, and they sent this in encrypted form to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The reports that came to the Main Staff from the corps, were those also in encrypted form or did that depend on the situation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most often they were sent in encrypted form.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would reports from the forward command posts come to the same organ as the reports from the corps, the operations sector, in other words?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In addition to the receipt of written reports from subordinate units, did the commander General Mladic also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt him. I'm not sure I understood the last question and answer: "Q. Would reports from the forward command post come to the same organ as the reports from the corps, the operations sector, in other words? "A. Yes." If it is addressed to their organ, or does it mean that any report from the IKM go to any command? Could you clarify?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course I could, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was there a particular sector that received reports -- particular Main Staff sector that received reports from the corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I explained that in the previous trial. Within the administration for operations and training, in addition to the operations department and the training department, it was envisaged by establishment to have a third body that was called the operations centre. According to establishment, it was supposed to have a higher ranking officer as the head of this centre and to higher ranking officers as shift leaders. Since we did not have enough personnel, this centre never became operational. So all these reports from the corps, from the anti-aircraft, from the schools, and so on, and forward command posts came to the Main Staff, addressed to the Main Staff, to the staff sector, to the administration for operations and training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it that that organ or that unit receives all the reports addressed to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In addition to these written reports from all these units, did General Mladic also have direct contact with the corps commanders?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had direct communication with corp commands. That was envisaged by the rules and instructions, and he had direct communication with all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And similarly, did he have direct communication with forward command posts for particular operations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were not permanent, but he did have relay communication with certain protection involving encryption.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This direct communication with the corps commands, you referred to it being envisaged by the rules and instructions.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: These are stationary communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did they occur with any regularity?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, once they were established, they were there throughout. Command posts of corps did not physically change their positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, we are on some irregular schedule today. If it is convenient, we will take a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, any time, Your Honour. I had no idea when the break might be so I just thought I would continued until warned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will take the break for half an hour and resume at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, just to continue where we left off before the break, I understood you to be saying that once the lines were established, General Mladic was in, effectively, permanent communication with the corps commanders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Every point in time he had the possibility of having direct communication with his subordinate commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did he do that by using any special system?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was a very ordinary Iskra switchboard, and when he'd press a button without dialling a dial, he could communicate with the commanders when they were at the headquarters of their respective corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just for those people who don't quite understand what Iskra means, maybe you could explain. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It's the make, the manufacturer from Slovenia that was called Iskra, from the town of Kranj.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, how often or was there a routine to how often General Mladic would speak with the corps commanders? Did he do it every day, every second day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot speak about each and every day specifically. Perhaps every afternoon towards the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And similarly, do you have any idea how often he might speak with forward command posts?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that, because I was not there sitting with the commander, so I cannot -- I mean, it's someone who was with him all the time that could answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What forward command post did you mean, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I was referring to those that the general had mentioned shortly before we broke, and I'll just, with your indulgence for a second, scroll back up to see the reference. I'll clarify. The reference was at page 77, line 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In the event one of the assistant commanders was deployed to a forward command post for a particular operation, do you have any idea how often General Mladic would be in contact with the assistant commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I can speak specifically about the point in time when I was at the western front, Jasenica and Drvar. Usually when this assistant commander would return from the field, reports would be written once they were received from units, and they would be formulated so as to be sent to the Main Staff. The commander would sometimes call the forward command post via safe communication equipment the commander, in this specific case, General Milovanovic, and ask about the situation in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you so often, but let me be clear. To understand the meaning of deployment, what I understood from your evidence, General, is that assistant commander can be sent out to field. For example, to monitor or to control whatever, and then he can use the facilities in the forward command post to communicate with his commander. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The forward command posts were established with a view to having direct insight into and influence over combat operations. At these forward command posts, all types of communications are organised like at basic command posts, except that they're on a smaller scale. I specifically spoke about the time when I was at the western --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then were you said to be deployed at that specific forward command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West -- I'm sorry, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This system you've just spoken about for communication with the corps commanders where General Mladic would press a button, was that a protected means of communication, free from interception?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: We believed that it was a protected means of communication, but how protected it actually was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just in terms -- or still on the subject of communication with assistant commanders, would the Main Staff have briefings? Would the Main Staff sectors and administration heads depicted in that organigramme gather for briefings with the commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: At certain points in time when necessary and when the commander would ask for such a meeting, yes. Within the sector and other sectors within their own sectors, we had meetings every morning discussing our work.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know how often the inner circle of the command, if I can call it that, would meet to discuss issues?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say. Probably they were held often without my being aware of it. It's very few people involved. At some office, at the commander's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think the last part of your answer wasn't heard. What I see you've said is, "At some office, at the commander's." Would you like to add to that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, either at the commander's or in one of offices of one of the assistant commanders or of the Chief of Staff or the assistant for morale, logistics, et cetera. These are six or seven people plus the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The Main Staff's daily combat reports, those sent to -- particularly those sent to the supreme commander and the corps commands that you discussed in your Tolimir testimony, how frequently were those sent?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The daily operative combat reports were sent as follows: One for the preceding 24 hours, that is to say it pertained to the 24 hours that had elapsed. These are regular reports, whereas extraordinary reports were sent when necessary, and in that way subordinate units reported to the command, the Main Staff, about the situation in their respective areas of responsibility, that is to say about the enemy, about their own forces, about neighbours, and about decisions taken by commanders, and of course they pointed out what the requirements and needs of their corps were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So reports were sent to the supreme commander on a daily basis. Do I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would the supreme commander also be sent extraordinary reports when necessary?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: If an extraordinary report would arrive from a corps, we would incorporate it into the next one, or if there was something important -- well, I did not have that kind of a situation that in my presence an extraordinary report would be sent especially to the commander and to other corps. For the most part, they were sent all together.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were they transmitted by secure means?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: They were transmitted through secure means, encrypted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we should intervene in the transcript. The witness said to the Supreme Command, not to the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Could you clarify, General Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We sent reports to the supreme commander. We addressed them to the supreme commander. However, they went also to the Ministry of Defence, to the president of the Assembly, the prime minister, and the minister of the interior, as well as to the forward command posts and all corps commands for their information so that they would be informed of the situation in the entire theatre of war. Now, here the question was about these extraordinary or interim reports. I did not take part in any forwarding of such reports, and that couldn't be the case anyway before the Chief of Staff was informed of it, because this interim report was meant to be resolved, so if it was resolved by the chief of staff then there was no reason for it to be sent to the Supreme Command. That would depend on the contents of the interim combat report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, whether the information that was contained in the interim combat report was of interest to the Supreme Command or whether it was just of relevance to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one question relating to your earlier answer: How do you know that these reports were sent to the minister of defence, the president of the Assembly, the prime minister, and the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know because at one point in time all of these instances were mentioned in the address block, and then it would say to the command of subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would the assistant commanders also receive copies of these reports?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were not addressed to them unless they were at the forward command post, and then they would receive it as the corps command for the entire -- a bit of information for the entire theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in addition to these written reports, do you know whether the commander or other members of the Main Staff had meetings with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that they did, but I can't really say with certainty. If there was a meeting of the Supreme Command and if representatives of the Main Staff were invited to that meeting, then they would be there; if not, they wouldn't. But I don't know. I don't have information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for just a moment, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, hearing your answer to that question, I thought I might turn to a transcript of your evidence given when you appeared as a Defence witness in the Popovic case, and I see at page 28244 you were asked by Mr. Petrusic: "General, do you have any knowledge whether the representatives of the command of the Main Staff have meetings with the civilian state leadership of the Republika Srpska, the government of the Republika Srpska?" And your answer was: "Yes." Do you remember that question and that answer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I think it had to do with -- it was within the context of an analysis of combat readiness, and when such analysis were discussed, then there would be political representatives attending.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll leave that for the moment but come back to it in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we get the reference again for that transcript page from the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's on the transcript. It says 28244.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it correct? Could you please help with us a line citation?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course. Lines 1 to 6.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In addition to these written reports and the meetings you've just referred to, did General Mladic or other members of the Main Staff have direct telephone contact with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: They did have a communication line. Now, whether it was a direct line or whether they had to use the PTT lines, I don't know, but they were at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just to go back to those written reports for a moment before moving forward, you indicated that they were sent by secure means. Would that imply that all the recipients would have had some way of protecting that information or decoding that information at the other end?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think it was printed out at one spot and then from there it was disseminated to other addresses, taken there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When those reports were sent to Pale, to the supreme commander, where would they be sent to and what then would happen to them next?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you just said that they were printed out at one spot and from there it was disseminated to other addresses. So my question is: What was the spot at Pale they were printed out at?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It was the seat of the government. They would have had to have some kind of communication unit that would have encryption equipment, and then once it was printed out it would be done at that one spot because not every minister would have one of these encryption machines. This is my assumption. I don't know exactly how it worked, but I assume they don't have so many -- they didn't have so many encryption devices there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now just a question again about communications. Based on your field experience that you talked about in your Tolimir testimony where you were deployed to the command post at the western front, did Dr. Karadzic have direct contact with the assistant commander on that occasion or during that period because it was a lengthy deployment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the Tolimir case I spoke about the general practice, which was that at the forward command post, they would have communications established towards the Main Staff and other points, but I wasn't present to witness possible communications between General Milovanovic and the president.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These reports that were disseminated, I think you would agree, were of a very detailed nature; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were lengthy.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could the president issue orders based on the information in those reports?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My remark was that this was a leading question, and it did not make it into the transcript. That was my prior remark to the previous question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You mean lengthy?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Line 13. No detailed nature. The previous question in interpretation I received that it was a leading question: You would agree, wouldn't you, that they were of a very detailed nature; correct? The question should have been: Were they detailed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed. The witness answered anyway. Ms. Edgerton, I was looking at the previous set of question and answer. You mentioned a communication with assistant commander, but the general spoke about General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I apologise for not naming him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were you satisfied with his answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. But I take it General Milovanovic was not one of the assistant commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, when I referred to communications with the assistant commander during your deployment to the western front, did you understand me to be referring to General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I was at a forward command post only where -- in a situation where he was the leading commander there, and per establishment, he's also the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And within the Main Staff, within the corps of the Main Staff, did General Milovanovic have the designation "assistant commander"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, the chief sector, the staff chief of sector for logistics, for moral guidance, for personnel, security and intelligence and these two independent administrations, planning, development, and finance, and air force and air defence, they were referred to as assistant commanders. However, General Milovanovic per establishment was the Chief of the Main Staff, and at the same time he was the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. To move back to these reports that we've been discussing, could the president issue orders based on the information contained in these reports?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The contents of the report would not be the decisive factor in whether the president would order it or not. He had the discretion to bypass the Main Staff, but how it went, I don't know the details. But generally speaking and under the rules of service, the second-in-line commander could issue an assignment to the second subordinate, and he could say that he received such and such a task from the second in command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you just explain for us, please, second-in-line commander, what you mean by second-in-line commander and second subordinate? It might be easier to do that by reference to their titles.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: For instance, let's take the 1st Krajina Corps. The commander of the 1st Krajina command -- Krajina Corps has as the first superior the commander of the Main Staff, and his second in command is the supreme commander. In other words, the supreme commander can issue an assignment to the 1st Krajina Corps, but the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps would have to inform of that his immediate superior, in other words, the commander of the Main Staff, that he had been issued such and such an assignment or a task from the supreme commander. Now, whether there were such instances of bypassing the immediate superior within the chain of command, I don't know, but I just talked about this as general possibilities within the rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Even if the immediate superior had been bypassed in the issuing of an order by the president, would the recipient of that order nevertheless be duty-bound to comply with it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's just what I've tried to explain. He is duty-bound to implement that order, but at the same time, he would have to report immediately to his immediate supreme -- to his immediate commander of this assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to actually look at a document, please, 65 ter 07514. It's an order dated 24 April 1994, from Dr. Karadzic to the Main Staff, the commander, and the Chief of Staff personally, and members of the Main Staff, and corps commanders for information, responding to their report. Now, General, I know you've seen this document the day before yesterday in preparation for your testimony today, but because it's a bit of a lengthy one, I wonder if you could take a few minutes to go through the couple of pages that it is and tell us when you've had a chance to have a look at it. And could you make the English side a little bit smaller, please, so we can see the full page, if you can. If you can scroll down just a little bit now. Do you remember seeing this in preparation for your testimony here today, General?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we go over now to the next page of this document. Now, General, this document refers to a number -- or this order refers to a number of things, including a withdrawal of forces of the Army of Republika Srpska, the disposition of heavy weapons, the equipping and disposition of mobile weapons, and the consolidation of positions. On receiving such an order, would the Main Staff then normally issue further orders and communications to subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please go back to page 1. In this order we see that the addressees are the Main Staff of the VRS, and then to the commander and Chief of the Main Staff personally, and then on line 3, it says: "For information to members of the Main Staff and all corps commanders." In other words, this order makes it obligatory to the Main Staff to inform thereof the most responsible members of the Main Staff and the corps commanders of this order. I don't know exactly when this was. I see that it is dated the 24th of April, 1994. I was not in the Main Staff then, so I don't know whether it was sent in writing or how it was communicated, but the command of the Main Staff was duty-bound to implement it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could just go down to paragraph 3 of this document that refers to convoy movement and the instruction that these convoys will be authorised by --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see that part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian that should be on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is there anyway of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is it just me or is there anyway we can have the English as well as the B/C/S version, because -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Third page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you see the line at the bottom of the third paragraph that says: "... these convoys will be authorised by a co-ordinating body, and the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska will be kept informed"?
