utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I want you to recall in your Tolimir testimony at page 12022, you explained that -- you explained the process for requests for convoy movement by UNPROFOR and international humanitarian organisations and you said that all convoy requests were received by fax in the department headed by Djurdjic, and he took them to the commander for approval. It was up to the commander to approve these requests or not to approve them. So I'm wondering, actually, how this document and mention of the co-ordinating body fits with your explanation about the processing of convoy requests within the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The UNHCR convoys and UNPROFOR convoys were the types of convoys that existed. UNPROFOR was -- was a peacekeeping military formation, whereas the UNHCR was humanitarian aid, and it was approved by the co-ordinating body.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So then what was the relationship between the co-ordinating body and the department for civilian affairs within the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: This co-ordinating body informed by fax which convoys and along which routes and what their destination was were approved and -- or whether they were not approved. And as for the UNPROFOR supply convoys, approval for them came from the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge of this co-ordinating body?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I believe Professor Koljevic was. I'm not absolutely certain, but I think it was him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could this be a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4447.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Registrar is kindly requested to repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4447.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go to another document related to convoy movement, 65 ter 03512. It's correspondence from the VRS Main Staff to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and Drina Corps command dated 6 March 1995. This document informs the corps commands of convoys which have been approved and instructs them to inform the check-points in order to prevent unapproved movement. Now that we've got the document on the screen in front of us, General, I'd actually like us to go to the signature block on the very last page, please. Now, General, this document has got General Miletic's signature block, and just above that is a line that reads in your language "zastupa nacelnika staba," which I understand means "standing in for the Chief of Staff"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: That is what it should mean. However, during my previous testimonies, I did say that I have never seen an order on this kind of standing in. There was no need for that because the Chief of Staff was never absent from the territory of Republika Srpska. Perhaps this was just incorrectly written. However, a stand-in commander would have all the powers that the office that he represents should have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How -- could you -- because we looked at a large number of documents issued or signed by General Miletic in this way the day before yesterday, I wonder if you could explain in a little bit more detail this term "standing in," and perhaps in that regard I could just ask you one question. What kind of circumstances -- in what kind of circumstances would someone be asked to stand in for a commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The commander has to have someone to stand in for him if he is prevented from carrying out his duties for a certain period of time. An order has to be written on having a person stand in for the commander in this way, and that is in accordance with the Law on the Army. A person who also has to stand in commander, in addition to his regular duties, has all the authorities and powers of the position that he is in as a standing commander, measures of reward, repression, everything. Here, specifically, General Milovanovic is present in the area of responsibility of the Army of Republika Srpska. He probably did give some kind of authority, but he should not have said "zastupa." It should have said "for the Chief of Staff" or "in accordance with the order of the Chief of Staff." As far as I know, no such order was ever written, and General Miletic did not have the powers that the Chief of Staff has. He could sometimes tell him to organise something within the work of the staff sector, but not both of them could have the powers of the Chief of Staff, and they are -- and they are present there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So then in this context, what kind of freedom of action would General Miletic have?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: What the Chief of Staff would give him, tell him, that he should stand in for him in some domains of his work, but he would certainly not transfer all authority to him. If you remember my CV, it says at some point in time, in addition to being the Chief of Staff of the 327th Brigade, I also stood in for the commander in his position two times during six-month periods, and I enjoyed all benefits then, the benefits and everything that is given to a commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in this context, in General Miletic's context, do I understand you to be saying he's limited by directions he receives from the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in the process of convoy requests, review and approval that you described in your Tolimir testimony, at what point would a direction like this to the corps have issued? And I wonder if we could go back to the first page in both languages, please. Top of the page in B/C/S. What -- in other words, what happens to a convoy request before a document like this issues?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this department for civilian affairs that is attached to the commander as it says here, they receive fax messages. Now, whether they are weekly -- I mean, are requests submitted weekly or does it happen every time a convoy is supposed to pass, then Colonel Milos Djurdjic, the head of this department, would collect all of these requests and go to see the commander. The commander would look at all of them together with him, and then perhaps he could say a few things to him in relation to that activity, because that is the only thing that he did, that Djurdjic did. And the commander on the margin of these faxes wrote that he approved of this or that he imposed certain restrictions with regard to the passage of convoys. When they would go through all these documents, then the other man would go back to the department and write up this kind of document. This was open communication. That is what it says up here, above Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And then when he would write that information that had to do with the mentioned units, then since the Chief of Staff would not be there, then he would go to General Miletic for him to sign it because his right was to communicate with subordinates just in that way. He could sign this information, only Colonel Djurdjic did not have this kind of authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just two questions, quick questions about the -- a couple of notations on the document. First of all, the number that appears above the date, number 06/18-104, does that number designate anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I think that that's the number of the log-book of Djurdjic's department.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what about the first number, 06? Does that mean anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: That is a designation of the department. I don't know exactly now. I cannot remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we can just --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: So if you look at this total number, 104, you see, 106/18, that is the department. And then -104, that is the 104th number in the log-book. So it was registered under that number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can just display the handwritten notes. At the top of the page for the General. Right there. General, what do those handwritten words Bresa, Domar, and Caura mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: These are code-names of brigades that are the addressees to whom this document is being sent. These are code-names, secret names.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And finally, can we just go down to item 5 on this list in both languages, please. The last question on this document, General. Could you have a look at item 5 on this list and tell me whether you see any military reason for the Main Staff to be concerned with the passage of a convoy between Sarajevo and Kiseljak, the one listed here, which was to supply drinks, suites, and potato chips for the canteen.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say. It has to do with provisions for the canteen, and that is a military catering facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this document as a Prosecution exhibit, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4448, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would next move into one more document which would take probably more time than we have. I'll do whatever I'm instructed, but I was just having a quick look at the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for today. We resume tomorrow morning at 9.00, General Obradovic. Oh, yes, we are sitting, because of some certain circumstances, we will resume at 1.30. Probably you are aware of this, but you are not supposed to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of February, 2012, at 1.30 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.59 p.m.,
